opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be a little careful with the word "emergence." There's been some nice work showing that a lot of what looks like sudden, discontinuous jumps in capability is partly an artifact of how we measure. If you score a task with an all-or-nothing metric, like exact match on a multi-step arithmetic problem, then the underlying competence can be improving smoothly with scale while the measured accuracy sits near zero and then shoots up. Switch to a metric that gives partial credit, like per-token log-likelihood, and much of that sharp transition smooths out.

That said, I don't think it's *all* a measurement illusion. These models are trained to predict the next token across an enormous, heterogeneous corpus, and to do that well you eventually have to pick up the regularities that generate the text: some syntax, some world knowledge, some patterns of reasoning that appear in the data. Different skills presumably need different amounts of capacity and data before the model can represent them reliably, so as you scale, you cross thresholds for various competencies at different points. Some of those competencies compose, and when they do, you can get qualitatively new behavior from combining pieces that were each learned gradually.

What worries me as a scientist is that we're mostly characterizing this from the outside, by running benchmarks. We don't have a good theory that would let us predict, before training a model, which capabilities will appear at which scale. That matters a lot for safety and deployment. If capabilities can appear in ways we didn't anticipate, then our evaluation practices need to be much more systematic. We need to test for competencies we're not expecting, not only the ones we designed for. It also matters for reliability: a capability that just crossed a threshold is often brittle, working on some phrasings and failing on others.

So my short answer is that it's a mix of smooth improvement in underlying representations, thresholded metrics that make it look abrupt, and real compositional effects. The research agenda I'd push is to open up the models: use interpretability tools to see what internal structures form as we scale, and connect that to the training data. Then "emergence" would become something we can explain and predict, not something we just observe after the fact.

r001.rationale: The response mentions competencies combining into new behavior, but does not explain that a sudden gain can occur when the model acquires the final prerequisite in a required combination.

r002.rationale: It says there is no good theory to predict which capabilities will appear at which scale before training.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing I'd say is that we should be a little careful with the word "sudden." There's been some nice work, for example the paper by Rylan Schaeffer and colleagues at Stanford, arguing that a lot of what looks like emergence is really an artifact of how we measure things. If you use a discontinuous metric like exact-match accuracy, where the model gets zero credit until it produces the entire correct answer, then a capability that is actually improving smoothly underneath will look like it appears out of nowhere once the model crosses some threshold. When you switch to a continuous metric, like the log probability assigned to the correct answer, the curve often becomes quite smooth. So some fraction of the "emergence" story is a measurement illusion.

That said, I don't think that fully explains it away. Many real tasks are compositional. To do multi-step arithmetic or to follow a chain of reasoning, you need several sub-skills to all be reliable at the same time. If each component has, say, a ninety percent success rate and the task requires six of them in sequence, you get about fifty percent overall. Each component improving gradually with scale can still produce a fairly sharp transition in the end-to-end task, because the product of those probabilities goes from near zero to usable rather quickly. So from the perspective of the person running the benchmark, it genuinely does look like a phase change, even though nothing discontinuous is happening inside the network.

The other piece I'd emphasize is the data. As you scale the model and the training set together, you're adding rarer and rarer phenomena to the data distribution. A capability like translating between two low-resource languages may just not have enough examples to be learned until you get to a certain data scale. So part of what we call emergence is the model finally having enough evidence to pick up patterns that were always there but very sparse.

What worries me, and I think this is the practical point, is that we don't yet have a good predictive theory. We can draw scaling laws for the loss quite accurately, but the mapping from loss to specific downstream capabilities is poorly understood. That means we can't reliably say in advance which abilities the next model will have, and that includes abilities we might not want. So I view emergence less as a mystery about the models and more as a symptom of how immature our science of evaluation and prediction still is. We need much finer-grained, mechanistic measures of what the model has learned, not just a handful of benchmark numbers, if we want to anticipate these transitions rather than be surprised by them.

r001.rationale: It explains that a multi-step task depends on several subskills becoming reliable together, so gradual improvements can produce a sharp gain once the combination is sufficient.

r002.rationale: It says there is no good predictive theory and that we cannot reliably say in advance which abilities the next model will have.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of things we need to separate. One is whether the model’s underlying ability is changing abruptly, and the other is whether our way of measuring that ability makes it look abrupt.

Suppose a task requires several steps, and you only give the model credit if it gets the entire answer right. As the model improves, it may be getting more of those steps right, but the score stays near zero. Then, once it becomes reliable enough, the score rises quite rapidly. That can look like a new capability suddenly appeared, even though the underlying improvement was gradual.

But that doesn’t mean every case is just a measurement effect. It’s also possible that a larger model learns a useful internal representation that a smaller model doesn’t, and that representation supports a whole collection of tasks. The difficult scientific question is figuring out which explanation applies in a particular case.

So I would want to look beyond the headline benchmark score. Can we measure partial progress? Can we identify what the model has learned? Can we predict when the capability will appear? Calling something ‘emergent’ describes the observation, but it doesn’t, by itself, explain the mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response describes gradual improvement across several steps producing a sharp score rise, but does not say the gain comes from acquiring the final prerequisite capability in a required combination.

r002.rationale: It asks whether we can predict when a capability will appear, but does not clearly acknowledge that predicting which capabilities emerge as models scale is difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between a capability emerging suddenly and our measurement of that capability changing suddenly. If you score a task as either completely correct or completely wrong, a model may be improving steadily underneath, but you won’t see that improvement until it crosses the threshold needed to get the whole answer right. Then it looks like a dramatic jump.

There could also be real qualitative changes as models scale. A larger model may be able to represent a useful computation that a smaller one cannot, or training may discover a strategy that suddenly makes a whole class of problems easier. But observing a jump in a benchmark doesn’t, by itself, tell us which explanation is right.

What I’d like to see is a more detailed account of what changes: look at partial progress, look across different examples and training runs, and test whether the capability is robust. That’s how we move from saying, ‘Something surprising happened,’ to understanding the mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response says steady improvement can become visible when performance crosses a task threshold, but it does not explain the gain as acquiring the final prerequisite in a combination of capabilities.

r002.rationale: The response notes uncertainty about what causes an observed jump, but does not say that predicting which capabilities will emerge as models scale is difficult.
